source_text: Οὐκ ἄρα ἡ πρόσοψις τοῦ ἐκτὸς ἀνθρώπου, ἀλλὰ ἡ ψυχὴ καλλωπιστέα τῷ τῆς καλοκἀγαθίας κοσμήματι· εἴη δ᾿ ἂν καὶ τὴν σάρκα εἰπεῖν τῷ τῆς ἐγκρατείας κόσμῳ. αἳ δέ, τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν καλλωπιζόμεναι καὶ τὰ βάθη χερσούμεναι, λελήθασι σφᾶς αὐτὰς κατὰ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίων κοσμοῦσαι ναούς· προπύλαια παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς καὶ προτεμενίσματα ἐξήσκηται, ἄλση τε καὶ ὀργάδες, κίοσίν τε παμπόλλοις ἐστεφάνωνται αἱ αὐλαί· τοῖχοι δὲ ἀποστίλβουσι ξενικοῖς λίθοις καὶ γραφῆς ἐντέχνου [οἷς] ἐνδεῖ οὐδὲ ἕν· χρυσῷ δὲ καὶ ἀργύρῳ καὶ ἠλέκτρῳ παραστίλβουσιν οἱ ναοί, καὶ τοῖς ἀπὸ Ἰνδίας καὶ Αἰθιοπίας πεποικιλμένοι μαρμαίρουσι λιθιδίοις, τὰ δὲ ἄδυτα χρυσοπάστοις ἐπισκιάζεται πέπλοις· ἀλλ᾿ ἢν παρεισέλθῃς εἰς τὸ βάθος τοῦ περιβόλου σπεύδων ἐπὶ τὴν θέαν τοῦ κρείττονος, ζητήσεις τὸ ἄγαλμα τὸ ἔνοικον τοῦ νεώ, παστοφόρος δὲ ἤ τις ἄλλος τῶν ἱεροποιούντων περὶ τὸ τέμενος σεμνὸν δεδορκώς, παιᾶνα τῇ Αἰγυπτίων ᾄδων γλώττῃ, ὀλίγον ἐπαναστείλας τοῦ καταπετάσματος, ὡς δείξων τὸν θεόν, πλατὺν ἡμῖν ἐνδίδωσι γέλωτα τοῦ σεβάσματος. οὐ γὰρ θεὸς ὁ ζητούμενος ἔνδον εὑρεθήσεται, ἐφ᾿ ὃν ἐσπεύσαμεν, αἴλουρος δὲ ἢ κροκόδειλος ἢ αὐτόχθων ὄφις ἤ τι τοιοῦτον θηρίον ἀνάξιον μὲν τοῦ νεώ, χηραμοῦ δὲ ἢ φωλεοῦ ἢ βορβόρου ἀντάξιον· ὁ θεὸς Αἰγυπτίων ἐπὶ στρωμνῆς ἁλουργῆς καταφαίνεται κυλιόμενον θηρίον. ταύτῃ μοι δοκοῦσιν αἱ χρυσοφοροῦσαι γυναῖκες, τῶν πλοκάμων τοὺς ἐνουλισμοὺς ἀσκοῦσαι χρίσματά τε παρειῶν καὶ ὑπογραφὰς ὀφθαλμῶν καὶ βαφὰς μετιοῦσαι τριχῶν καὶ τὴν ἄλλην βλακείαν κακομηχανώμεναι, κοσμοῦσαι τὸν περίβολον τὸν σαρκικόν, αἰγυπτιάζουσαι ὡς ἀληθῶς, ἐπισπᾶσθαι τοὺς δεισιδαίμονας ἐραστάς. ἀλλ᾿ ἢν ἀποκαλύψῃ τις τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ νεώ, τὸν κεκρύφαλον λέγω, τὴν βαφήν, τὴν ἐσθῆτα, τὸ χρυσίον, τὸ φῦκος, τὰ ἐντρίμματα, τουτέστι τὸ ἐκ τούτων συγκείμενον ὕφος, [τὸ καταπέτασμα,] ὡς ἔνδον εὑρήσων τὸ κάλλος τὸ ἀληθινόν, μυσάξεται, εὖ οἶδ᾿ ἐγώ. οὐ γὰρ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ θεοῦ κατοικοῦσαν ἔνδον εὑρήσει τὴν ἀξιόλογον, πόρνη δὲ ἀντ᾿ αὐτῆς καὶ μοιχαλὶς τῆς ψυχῆς κατείληφε τὸ ἄδυτον, τό τε ἀληθινὸν θηρίον ἐλεγχθήσεται ψιμυθίῳ πίθηκος ἐντετριμμμένος, καὶ ὁ παλίμβολος ὄφις ἐκεῖνος διαβιβρώσκων τὸ νοερὸν τῆς ἀνθρώπου διὰ τῆς φιλοδοξίας χηραμὸν ἔχει τὴν ψυχήν· πάντα φαρμάκων ὀλεθρίων ἐμπλήσας καὶ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τῆς πλάνης ἐνερευξάμενος ἰὸν μετεσκεύασεν τὰς γυναῖκας εἰς πόρνας ὁ προαγωγὸς οὗτος δράκων (οὐ γὰρ γυναικός, ἀλλ᾿ ἑταίρας τὸ φιλόκοσμον)· αἳ τῆς παρὰ μὲν τοῖς ἀνδράσιν οἰκουρίας ὀλίγα φροντίζουσιν, λύσασαι δὲ τἀνδρὸς τὸ βαλλάντιον ἐκτρέπουσι τὰς χορηγίας εἰς ἐπιθυμίας, ὡς πολλοὺς ἔχοιεν τοῦ καλαὶ δοκεῖν εἶναι μάρτυρας, καὶ τὴν πᾶσαν ἡμέραν κομμωτικῇ προσκαθεζόμεναι ἀργυρωνήτοις σχολάζουσιν ἀνδραπόδοις. καθάπερ οὖν ὄψον πονηρὸν ἡδύνουσι τὴν σάρκα καὶ τὴν μὲν ἡμέραν κομμωτικῇ προστετήκασι θαλαμευόμεναι, μὴ ἐλεγχθῶσιν ξανθιζόμεναι, ἑσπέρας δὲ καθάπερ ἐκ φωλεοῦ πρὸς τὸν λύχνον τὸ νόθον τοῦτο προσέρπει κάλλος· συνεργεῖ γὰρ καὶ ἡ μέθη καὶ τὸ ἀμυδρὸν τοῦ φωτὸς πρὸς τὴν ἐπίθεσιν αὐτῶν.
pass_a_gloss: Not, then, the face of the outer man, but the soul is to be adorned with the ornament of goodness and beauty; and let it even be said that the body also is to be adorned with the ornament of self-control. But those who adorn the surface and neglect the depths, have forgotten themselves, just as the Egyptians adorn their temples; they have propylaea and prostyle temples, and groves and orchards, and the courts are crowned with many wreaths; the walls shine with foreign stones and artistic inscriptions, which are not even needed; and the temples shine with gold and silver and ivory, and are adorned with variegated stones from India and Ethiopia; and the innermost parts are shaded with golden canopies. But if you enter into the depth of the enclosure, hastening to the sight of what is superior, you will seek the statue that dwells in the temple, and one of the priests, or some other of the temple servants, having opened a little of the curtain, as if to show the god, will display to us the laughable object of reverence. For the god that is sought will not be found within, for which we hastened, but a cat or a crocodile or an indigenous snake, or some such animal, unworthy of the temple, but worthy of a dung-hill or a hole or a sewer; the god of the Egyptians appears as a rolling animal on a purple couch. In the same way, it seems to me, the women who wear gold, having anointed their hair-styles and having written on their faces and having dyed their eyebrows and having colored their hair, and having contrived other foolishness, adorn the fleshly enclosure, and, as it were, truly Egyptianizing, strive to attract the lovers who fear them. But if someone should uncover the veil of the temple, that is, the hair-style, the dye, the clothing, the gold, the purple, the ornaments, that is, the fabric composed of these things, as if to find the true beauty within, he will be disgusted, I know well. For he will not find the image of God dwelling within, worthy of honor, but a prostitute and adulteress of the soul has occupied the innermost part, and the true animal will be convicted of being a monkey smeared with cosmetics, and that versatile snake, passing through the mind of man through ambition, has the soul as its dung-hill; having filled everything with deadly poisons and having poured out the venom of his own deceit, this dragon, the promoter of corruption, has transformed the women into prostitutes (for the love of adornment is not of a wife, but of a harlot); who, having little concern for the household, according to the men, but having loosened the purse of the husband, turn their resources into desires, as if they had many witnesses to their beauty, and spend the whole day sitting at their cosmetics, idle with hired servants. Just as, then, bad food corrupts the flesh, and they have added the whole day to their cosmetics, hiding in their chambers, lest they be convicted of being yellow-haired, but in the evening, as if from a hole, this spurious beauty creeps towards the lamp; for drunkenness and the dimness of the light also cooperate with their assault.
pass_b_english: It is not the outward appearance of the body that must be adorned, but the soul, with the ornament of goodness and beauty; one might even say that the body should be adorned with the ornament of self-control. But women who beautify the surface while neglecting the depths have forgotten themselves, just as the Egyptians adorn their temples. Those temples have gateways and porticoes, groves and orchards, and their courts are crowned with countless wreaths. Their walls shine with exotic stones and artistic inscriptions that lack nothing; the shrines gleam with gold, silver, and ivory, and sparkle with variegated stones from India and Ethiopia, while their innermost sanctuaries are shaded by golden canopies. Yet if you press into the depths of the precinct, eager to see the greater thing, you will look for the indwelling statue. A priest or some other temple servant, looking solemn, will draw back a corner of the curtain as if to reveal the god, and will show you the ridiculous object of worship. For the god you sought will not be found within — the one you hurried to see — but a cat, or a crocodile, or a native snake, or some such creature, unworthy of the temple yet fit for a dung-heap, a den, or a sewer. The god of the Egyptians appears as a rolling beast on a purple couch.

In the same way, it seems to me, the gold-wearing women — anointing their elaborate hairstyles, painting their faces, dyeing their eyebrows, coloring their hair, and devising every other foolishness — adorn the fleshly enclosure, and by so doing they truly Egyptianize, striving to attract superstitious lovers. But if someone should pull back the veil of the shrine, that is, the hairstyle, the dye, the clothing, the gold, the purple, the ornaments — in short, the whole fabric woven from these things — expecting to find the true beauty within, he will be disgusted, I know well. For he will not find the honorable image of God dwelling inside, but a prostitute and adulteress of the soul has occupied the inner sanctuary. The true beast will be exposed as a monkey smeared with cosmetics, and that treacherous snake, slipping through the human mind by way of ambition, has made the soul its dung-heap. Having filled everything with deadly poisons and poured out the venom of his own deceit, this dragon, the promoter of corruption, has turned the women into harlots — for the love of adornment belongs not to a wife but to a courtesan. These women care little for the household duties that belong to wives, yet they loosen their husbands' purses and divert the household resources toward their own desires, as if they needed many witnesses to attest their beauty. They spend the whole day seated at their toilette, idle, attended by hired servants.

Just as bad food corrupts the flesh, so they devote the entire day to cosmetics, cloistered in their chambers lest they be caught looking sallow. But at evening, like something creeping from a hole, this counterfeit beauty steals toward the lamplight; for drunkenness and the dimness of the light both cooperate in their assault.
